The following text is adapted from Marisol Ekwueme's 2019 novel The Long Rows. Ines, an agricultural researcher, is visiting her test fields after a summer without rain.

Ines had driven out expecting to find nothing. The neighboring farms were brown to the fence line, their corn folded over like paper. But at the edge of her plots she stopped. The wheat she had spent six years crossing and recrossing stood upright, thin but green, its heads already filling. She knelt and pressed a stalk between her fingers, as if to be sure it was real, and found that she was laughing.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ines is relieved to discover that the wheat she developed has survived the drought.
Ines is discouraged to find that her test plots fared no better than nearby farms.
Ines worries that her neighbors will resent the success of her experimental crop.
Ines notices that the corn on neighboring farms has been damaged by the dry summer.
items.explanation: You follow Ines from expecting to find nothing to kneeling in disbelief and laughing. The turn at 'But' shows her wheat has survived when everything around it died, and her laughter shows relief and joy. Choice A matches both the situation and that emotional direction.

B.why: You reversed the tone. Ines expected failure, but the text says her wheat 'stood upright' and green while the nearby farms were brown. Her laughing shows the opposite of discouragement.

C.why: You added a motive the text never gives. Nothing suggests Ines is thinking about her neighbors' feelings. Their farms appear only as a contrast to her surviving wheat.

D.why: You picked a true detail from the second sentence, but it is too narrow. The dead corn is background that sets up the real focus: Ines's reaction to her own wheat.

The following text is from Tomasz Reyna's 2008 poem "Proof." The speaker is a printmaker.

All morning I cut the block by feel,
gouging the pale wood toward a shape
I carried backward in my head.
I rolled the ink, black and slow as tar,
laid the paper, leaned my weight on it.
Only when I peeled the sheet away
did I see what my hands had meant—
the heron, facing the right way at last,
more certain than I ever was.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker describes the tools and materials needed to cut and ink a woodblock.
The speaker is frustrated that the finished print differs from the image planned.
The speaker works without fully seeing the image until the finished print reveals it.
The speaker regrets choosing a medium that offers so little certainty to the artist.
items.explanation: In plain English: the speaker carves 'by feel' with the image held 'backward' in mind, and 'only when' the paper comes off does the heron appear clearly, 'more certain' than the speaker felt. The poem moves from working half-blind to seeing the image revealed, and choice C covers both parts.

A.why: You described only the images from the first lines (the block, the ink, the paper) and missed the turn at 'Only when,' where the poem arrives at its point.

B.why: You reversed the tone. The heron faces 'the right way at last.' The print shows what the speaker's hands 'had meant,' so it matches the speaker's intention rather than disappointing it.

D.why: You added a regret the poem never states. The speaker admits to uncertainty but never wishes for a different medium. The ending sounds like wonder, not regret.

The following text is adapted from Harriet Olumide's 2015 novel Census. Theo, a graduate student in ornithology, is conducting a morning bird count in a marsh.

Theo had been told the count would be tedious: three hours on a wet platform, tallying whatever flew past. By the first hour he had filled two pages. A pair of rails picked through the reeds below him; a harrier swung low over the water and was gone. He forgot the cold in his boots. When his supervisor's truck pulled up, Theo looked at his watch in disbelief. It seemed impossible that the morning was already over.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Theo finds the bird count just as tedious as others had warned him it would be.
Theo becomes so absorbed in the bird count that the morning passes unnoticed.
Theo hopes to impress his supervisor by recording more birds than expected.
Theo watches a harrier fly low over the marsh water before it disappears.
items.explanation: Theo was warned the count would be tedious, but he fills pages, forgets the cold, and can't believe the morning is over. Those are signs of someone absorbed in his work, and choice B captures that.

A.why: You took the warning in the first sentence as Theo's real experience. Everything after it, such as forgetting the cold and his 'disbelief' at the time, shows the count was the opposite of tedious.

C.why: You added a motive the text never gives. The supervisor shows up only to mark the end of the morning. Nothing says Theo is trying to impress anyone.

D.why: You chose one image from the middle of the passage. The harrier is one of many sights that hold Theo's attention, not the point of the passage.

The following text is adapted from Ansel Varga's 2021 novel Contour Lines. Lucía, a cartographer, is preparing a new map of the valley where she grew up.

Lucía had drawn hundreds of valleys, but never her own. The survey data arrived on a Tuesday, and she traced it as she would any other: the ridgeline, the river, the new reservoir spreading blue across the lower fields. Only when she began to letter the names did she pause. There was no label to give the square where her grandmother had kept goats, no road to mark to the schoolhouse. The water covered all of it. She set down her pen and did not pick it up again until evening.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Lucía is pleased to finally have the chance to map the valley where she grew up.
Lucía leaves the flooded village off the map to avoid upsetting her own family.
Lucía uses survey data to trace the ridgeline and river of a mountain valley.
Lucía is saddened when mapping her home valley shows that familiar places are gone.
items.explanation: Lucía starts out treating the job like any other, then stops when she sees that the places she remembers are under the reservoir. Putting down her pen until evening shows her grief. Choice D matches both the situation and the move toward loss.

A.why: You reversed the tone. The text never shows Lucía pleased. It builds toward her stopping work entirely because of what the water has covered.

B.why: You added a motive and an action the text never gives. The places are missing from the map because they are underwater, not because Lucía chose to hide them from anyone.

The following text is from Noor Castellanos's 2017 poem "Gauge." The speaker is a hydrologist who measures a river's height each spring.

Each spring I wade out to the gauge
and read the river by its rising marks,
the numbers climbing inch by inch
with snow that fell on peaks I'll never climb.
I write them down. I send them on.
But this year, standing waist-deep in the cold,
I felt the whole weight of the mountain's winter
pressing past my legs toward the sea,
and then, and only then, I understood
what all my columns had been counting.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker explains the procedure for recording a river's height every spring.
The speaker realizes, while doing a routine task, the force behind the numbers.
The speaker grows tired of measuring a river whose changes seem too small.
The speaker gives up recording data in favor of experiencing the river directly.
items.explanation: In plain English: every year the speaker reads the gauge and passes along the numbers, but this year, feeling the snowmelt push past, the speaker 'then, and only then' understands what those numbers stand for. Choice B includes both the routine and the realization it leads to.

C.why: You reversed the tone. The speaker feels 'the whole weight' of the river, not changes too small to matter, and the poem ends in understanding rather than weariness.

The following text is adapted from Desmond Achterberg's 2012 novel Load Paths. Walter, a retired civil engineer, is being driven across a bridge he helped design forty years earlier.

His granddaughter drove, chatting about her classes, and Walter let her talk. As the car climbed onto the span, he felt the old habit return: he listened for the joints, watched the cables, counted the lamp posts. Every one was where he had put it. Traffic streamed past in both directions, hundreds of people who had never heard his name and never needed to. Walter settled back in his seat and smiled. Forty years, and it was still holding everyone up.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Walter feels quiet pride that the bridge he designed still serves people so well.
Walter is anxious that the aging bridge may no longer be safe for drivers to cross.
Walter is hurt that the people crossing his bridge do not know who designed it.
Walter's granddaughter talks to him about her classes while she drives the car.
items.explanation: Walter checks the bridge out of old habit, finds everything where he put it, then settles back and smiles because it is 'still holding everyone up.' That is quiet pride in lasting work, which is choice A.

B.why: You read his listening and watching as worry. The text calls it 'the old habit,' and what he finds, every part where he put it, leads him to relax and smile rather than feel anxious.

C.why: You added a hurt feeling the text never gives. The drivers 'never needed to' know his name, and Walter smiles right after, so he is content, not wounded.

D.why: You chose a background detail from the first sentence. The granddaughter's chatter sets the scene, but the passage is about Walter's feelings toward the bridge.

The following text is adapted from Leela Arnaud's 2020 novel The Field Reels. Priya, a musicologist, is cataloging old field recordings in a university archive.

The reel was labeled only with a date and the name of a village. Priya threaded it onto the machine as she had threaded two hundred others that month, pencil ready for the catalog card. A woman's voice came through the hiss, unaccompanied, singing low. Priya's pencil stopped. items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Priya grows impatient with the slow, repetitive work of cataloging recordings.
Priya suspects that the reel was mislabeled and belongs to a different village.
Priya threads a reel onto the machine and prepares to fill out a catalog card.
Priya is deeply moved to recognize a song from her childhood in a recording.
items.explanation: Priya starts the reel as routine work, then her pencil stops when she recognizes her mother's song. Playing it three times before writing anything shows how moved she is. Choice D covers both the discovery and her feeling about it.

A.why: You fixed on 'two hundred others' and assumed boredom. The passage turns away from routine at the moment she hears the song, and she lingers over the recording instead of rushing through it.

B.why: You added a suspicion the text never gives. The sparse label is simply how the reel arrives. Priya's reaction is recognition, not doubt about where it came from.

The following text is from a poem. The speaker is looking at a distant star through a backyard telescope.

A white point, steady over the garden wall,
cold as a nail-head in the dark.
I learned tonight its light set out
before my grandmother was born.
So what I hold here in the glass

and I stand reading it long after

choices: The speaker reflects that the starlight is so old that the star may no longer exist.
The speaker describes how bright and cold the star looks above the garden wall.
The speaker is disappointed that the telescope shows the star as only a small point.
The speaker regrets never having shown this particular star to a beloved grandmother.

The following text is from an original short story. Nell keeps the wage ledger at a small shoe factory.

Nell had dreaded the first of the month for a year. Every payday the columns came out short, and every payday she had to tell someone that their hours had been cut. This month she added the totals twice, then a third time, not trusting them. The new contract had raised every rate. She closed the ledger, smoothed its cover with both hands, and found that she was smiling.
items.stem: Follow Nell's feeling from the start of the text to the end. Which choice best describes how it changes?
choices: Nell moves from dreading payday to feeling relieved about the higher wages.
Nell moves from feeling relieved about payday to dreading the higher wages.
Nell adds the totals three times because she doubts her own arithmetic skills.
Nell hides the new totals so that the workers will not ask for even more.
items.explanation: Find where the feeling starts and where it ends. At the start, Nell 'had dreaded the first of the month.' At the end, she 'found that she was smiling' after the new contract raised every rate. So her feeling goes from dread to relief. This one step, following a character's feeling from the first line to the last, is what you need for the Easy main-idea question on fiction excerpts. That question asks which choice best states the main idea, and its answer always matches the direction the feeling moves.

B.why: You picked up the right two feelings but put them in the wrong order. The dread comes first and the smile comes last. When you check the direction of a feeling, look at the final sentence to see where it ends up.

C.why: She does add the totals three times, but that is one line from the middle of the text, and it is about not trusting good news, not about her arithmetic. A choice built on one sentence leaves out how her feeling changes from start to end.

All summer the swifts stitched the sky above the chimney,

The following text is from an original short story. Tomás is an apprentice in a printmaking workshop.

Tomás had meant to carve only the border before lunch. But the cherry block took the gouge so cleanly that he kept going, curl after pale curl, into the leaves and then the bird's wing. He did not hear the bell or notice the light shift across the bench. When the master finally touched his shoulder, the windows were dark, and Tomás looked up, surprised to find the day gone.
items.stem: Follow Tomás's feeling from the start of the text to the end. Which choice best describes how he feels about his work?
choices: Tomás is bored by the carving and keeps waiting for the long day to end.
Tomás is so absorbed in the carving that he loses all track of the time.
Tomás carves well past dark so that he can hide his work from the master.
Tomás carves a block of cherry wood that shows a bird among some leaves.
items.explanation: Follow the feeling from start to end. Tomás meant to stop at lunch, but he 'kept going,' did not hear the bell, and was 'surprised to find the day gone.' Each detail shows the same thing: he is absorbed in the work. On the Easy main-idea question about fiction, the answer matches a feeling like this, one that the details build up together.

A.why: This reverses the tone. Someone who is bored watches the clock, but Tomás didn't hear the bell at all. Missing the time is a sign that he is absorbed, not that he is waiting for the day to end.

C.why: Nothing in the text says Tomás is hiding anything. The master walks up and touches his shoulder. You added a motive the text never gives.

D.why: This is a true detail, but it only tells you what he carved, not how he feels while carving. It leaves out the feeling that the whole passage builds toward.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is from an original memoir. The narrator is a marine biologist returning to a coral reef two years after a heat wave bleached it white.

I dropped into the water expecting a graveyard. Two years earlier the reef had been bone-white from end to end, and I had stopped telling people I studied it. However, near the base of the old brain corals, I found small brown knobs, new polyps, no bigger than my thumbnail. I counted forty before my air ran low. I surfaced laughing into my mask, already planning the next dive.
items.stem: Follow the narrator's feeling from the start of the text to the end. Which choice best describes how it changes?
choices: The narrator expects to find a recovering reef but is let down by its damage.
The narrator dives on a reef that was bleached white by a heat wave long ago.
The narrator concludes that the reef has fully healed and needs no more study.
The narrator expects to find a dead reef but grows hopeful on seeing regrowth.
items.explanation: The word 'However' marks the turn. Before it, the narrator expects 'a graveyard.' After it, the narrator finds new polyps and surfaces 'laughing,' already planning to come back. So the feeling goes from expecting the worst to feeling hopeful. On the Easy main-idea question about memoirs and stories, the answer usually follows whatever comes after a pivot like this one.

A.why: This swaps the expectation and the outcome. The narrator expected damage and found regrowth, not the other way around. Check which side of 'However' each feeling is on.

B.why: This comes from the italic introduction and the first two sentences only. It sets the scene, but it leaves out the change of feeling, which is the point of the passage.

C.why: Forty small polyps is a hopeful sign, not a full recovery. The narrator is already planning the next dive, which is the opposite of 'no more study.' This choice claims more than the text supports.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a short story about Ines, who has just finished her first week of work at a textile mill.

At the gate, the foreman handed Ines a brown envelope. She did not open it on the tram. At home she set it on the kitchen table and counted the coins twice, lining them up by size. Six days of threading bobbins, and here they were, small and solid. She sat back and smiled, feeling for the first time that her work was worth something.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ines feels proud when she receives the wages from her first week of work.
Ines feels let down by how small the wages from her first week of work are.
Ines keeps her first week's wages hidden so that no one else can take them.
Ines notices that the coins in her pay envelope come in different sizes.
items.explanation: The introduction tells you who Ines is and what is happening: she has just finished her first week at the mill. Now follow her feelings from start to end. She counts the coins carefully, she smiles, and the last sentence names the feeling directly: her work is 'worth something.' That is pride, and choice A covers both the situation (her first wages) and where her emotion ends up. This is the basic move behind every literary main-idea question: work out the situation, then follow the character's feeling to the end.

B.why: You took the word 'small' as a complaint and flipped the tone. The coins are 'small and solid,' and Ines smiles. Nothing in the text shows disappointment. Choices that reverse the character's feeling are the most common trap in this kind of question.

C.why: You added a motive the text never gives. Ines waits to open the envelope until she gets home, but the passage never says she is hiding it or worried that someone will take it. If you can't point to a line that states the motive, the choice is adding something the text doesn't say.

D.why: This is true, since she lines the coins up by size, but it describes only one small action. The passage is about what the wages mean to her. A choice can be accurate and still be too narrow to be the main idea.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from a novel. Ines, a nutrition scientist, is visiting her grandmother.

Ines had spent a decade counting grams of sodium for strangers, and she arrived at her grandmother's kitchen braced to disapprove. The stew was dark with salted pork; the bread had been fried in lard. She opened her mouth to say something about arteries. But her grandmother was humming as she ladled, and the neighbors crowding the table were laughing over one another, and Ines found that the lecture she had rehearsed on the train no longer seemed to belong in the room. She took a second bowl and said nothing.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ines, prepared to criticize the meal, decides that the nutritional advice she has given for years is mistaken.
Ines, prepared to criticize the meal, sets aside her objections once she experiences the warmth of the gathering.
Ines notices that her grandmother's stew and bread are made with salted pork and fried in lard.
Ines grows irritated by the noisy neighbors and decides to leave before the meal is over.
items.explanation: Follow Ines from start to end: she arrives 'braced to disapprove,' but after 'But' the humming grandmother and laughing neighbors make her lecture feel out of place, and she quietly takes a second bowl. Choice B gets both halves right: the situation (ready to criticize) and the direction her feeling takes (she lets the objection go because of the warmth in the room).

A.why: This is the half-right answer. The first half is accurate, but the text never says Ines thinks her science is wrong. She only decides this isn't the moment for a lecture. You stopped reading once you recognized the opening words.

C.why: This is true, but it covers just one sentence. It leaves out Ines's change of heart, which is what the whole passage builds toward. It is too narrow.

D.why: This gets the tone backwards. The laughter wins Ines over rather than annoying her, and she stays for a second bowl instead of leaving.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker, a sports scientist, is timing a young runner on a track.

The stopwatch knows her by hundredths: / stride length, ground contact, the angle / of a knee at the moment of push. / I have charted her for three seasons, / every figure tidier than the last. / Yet this morning, when she crossed the line / and threw her head back, laughing, into the wind, / I looked down and found I had forgotten / to press the button at all.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker describes the precise measurements used to track the runner's stride and form.
The speaker, who has measured the runner for years, regrets an error that spoiled a season of data.
The speaker grows frustrated that the runner's times have stopped improving after three seasons.
The speaker, who has measured the runner for years, is so moved by her joy that the timing is forgotten.
items.explanation: Put the poem into plain English. For three seasons the speaker has recorded this runner in exact detail. Then 'Yet' brings the turn: the runner crosses the line laughing, and the speaker is so caught up in the moment that they never stop the watch. Choice D covers the years of measuring and the turn at the end.

A.why: This only describes the images in the opening lines. It skips the turn after 'Yet,' which is what the poem is really about. That is the usual poetry trap.

B.why: The first half is right, but nothing in the poem suggests regret or lost data. It misses one timing on one morning, and the tone is wonder, not dismay. Read every choice to the end.

C.why: The poem says each figure was 'tidier than the last,' so the runner is getting better, and the speaker shows delight, not frustration.

The following text is from a short story. Priya, a public health officer, is writing the final report on a clean-water campaign she led.

The report was due Friday, and Priya had the numbers: cholera admissions down by two thirds, the new pumps working in eleven of twelve villages. The minister's office would want a photograph. She thought instead of the twelfth village, where the pump had cracked in the first frost and a woman had walked her, without complaint, to the old well her family still used. Priya typed the figures, looked at them for a long time, and then added a paragraph no one had asked for.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Although the campaign largely succeeded, Priya is unwilling to leave its one failure out of her report.
Although the campaign largely succeeded, Priya worries that the minister will blame her for the broken pump.
Priya records that the new pumps are working in eleven of the twelve villages in the campaign.
Priya is pleased that her report will present the campaign to the minister as a complete success.
items.explanation: The last sentence ties it together. Priya has strong numbers, but her mind keeps going back to the twelfth village. D.why: This reverses the ending. Priya adds the paragraph because she doesn't want the report to look like a complete success.

The following text is from a memoir. The author, a musicologist, describes transcribing old field recordings of folk songs.

For the first month I transcribed the tapes as I had been trained to: pitch, rhythm, the placement of each ornament, all of it pinned to the staff. The singers were long dead, and the hiss of the old reels made them sound farther away still. Then, on a recording from 1958, a woman stopped mid-verse to scold a child, laughed, and began the line again a half step higher. I did not notate the change. I rewound the tape and listened to her laugh, and then I listened again.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The author grows impatient with interruptions that make the old recordings difficult to transcribe.
The author's routine technical work gives way to a decision to abandon formal notation entirely.
The author's routine technical work gives way to fascination with a singer as a real person.
The author explains that one singer resumed her verse a half step higher than she began it.
items.explanation: Follow how the author feels over time. At first the work is mechanical and the singers seem far away. Then one woman's unplanned moment pulls the author in, and they stop notating and replay her laugh. Choice C describes that move from routine to fascination.

A.why: This gets the tone backwards. The interruption fascinates the author, who rewinds to hear it again rather than getting annoyed.

B.why: The first half is right, but the author skips notating one change on one tape. Nothing says they give up notation altogether. You stopped reading once you recognized the opening words.

D.why: This is accurate but covers only one detail. It leaves out the author's reaction, which is what the passage is building to.

A student uncovers a roof tile bearing a dog's paw print that was pressed in before the clay was fired.

Halloran, though familiar with such finds, chooses not to spoil the students' newly awakened wonder.

The following text is from a poem. The speaker, an immunologist, is looking at blood cells under a microscope.

Under the lens they are only shapes: / the macrophage slumped like a sack of grain, / the lymphocytes small and round as seeds. / I have named them all a thousand times. / But tonight, my own blood on the slide, / I watched one cell reach out and swallow / a thing that would have harmed me, / and I thanked it, aloud, alone in the lab, / as if it could hear.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker compares the shapes of familiar blood cells to everyday objects such as grain and seeds.
Seeing their own cells at work turns the speaker's routine observation into personal gratitude.
Seeing their own cells at work, the speaker fears that their immune system is beginning to fail.
The speaker concludes that immunologists should study patients' feelings as well as their cells.
items.explanation: Put the poem into plain English. The speaker has looked at these cells so often that they are 'only shapes.' Then 'But' brings the turn: it's the speaker's own blood, a cell destroys something harmful, and the speaker thanks it out loud. Choice B covers the routine and the gratitude it turns into.

A.why: This only describes the comparisons in the opening lines. It skips the turn after 'But,' which is where the poem's meaning is. That is the usual poetry trap.

C.why: The first half is right, but the cell is doing its job by destroying 'a thing that would have harmed me.' The speaker feels grateful, not afraid.

D.why: This turns a private moment into a lesson for the whole field. The poem never makes that claim.

The following text is from a novel. Ines, a county nurse, is going from farm to farm offering vaccinations during a diphtheria outbreak.

By the ninth farmhouse Ines had stopped counting the miles. Her satchel had grown heavy with unused vials, and at three doors she had been turned away before she could speak. Still, at each gate she paused to straighten her collar, as if the next family might be the first to listen. At the Pruitt place a girl of six came out alone, held out her arm without being asked, and watched the needle with grave interest. Ines drove home in the dark, tired to the bone, and found she was humming.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Though Ines's rounds are long and often met with refusal, one willing child leaves her quietly cheered at the end of the day.
Though Ines's rounds are long and often met with refusal, she keeps making them mainly to avoid disappointing the county doctor.
A young girl at the Pruitt farm accepts her vaccination calmly and holds out her arm before anyone has asked her to.
Ines grows bitter toward the families who turn her away and dreads each new gate she has to approach that day.
items.explanation: Follow Ines's feeling from start to end. The day is exhausting and discouraging (unused vials, three refusals), yet she keeps going with hope at every gate, and after the Pruitt girl's eager arm she drives home 'tired to the bone' and humming. Choice A covers both halves: the hard, rejected rounds and the lift that one receptive child gives her.

B.why: The first half matches A word for word, so you probably stopped reading there. The second half gives Ines a motive the text never mentions. No doctor appears, and nothing suggests she is working to avoid anyone's disapproval.

C.why: This is accurate, but it covers only one moment. It leaves out Ines, the long and discouraging day, and the way she feels at the end, so it is too narrow to be the main idea.

The following text is from a short story. Marisol, an apprentice in a print shop, is pulling the first print from a woodblock she has carved.

Marisol peeled the paper back slowly, bracing for the worst. The heron she had carved over three weeks came up crooked, its neck thicker than she had drawn it, and a stray gouge had left a white scar across the water. Old Teodoro would notice it at once. Yet the longer she looked, the less the scar resembled a mistake. It caught the light the way a ripple does. She pinned the sheet to the drying line and, for the first time that month, did not reach for a fresh block.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Marisol expects her first print to disappoint her but comes to value it, flaws included.
Marisol worries about Teodoro's judgment and decides to keep her flawed print hidden from him.
Marisol is frustrated by the flaws in her print and resolves to carve the heron again.
Marisol notices that a stray gouge in her block has left a white mark across the water.
items.explanation: Follow Marisol's feeling from start to end. She begins 'bracing for the worst' and lists the print's faults, then 'Yet' turns it: the scar stops looking like a mistake and starts to look like a ripple. The last sentence adds it up. She hangs the print and, for once, does not reach for a new block. So she moves from expecting disappointment to accepting the flawed print, and only A matches both the situation and that change.

B.why: The text does say Teodoro would notice the scar, but it never says Marisol plans to hide anything. She pins the print up on the drying line in plain view. You added a motive the passage doesn't give.

C.why: This gets the direction of her feeling backwards. The ending says that for the first time she did 'not reach for a fresh block,' so she is not going to carve the heron again. You stopped reading at the list of flaws, before the 'Yet' turn.

D.why: This is true, but it only covers one sentence. It describes a detail of the print and misses Marisol's change of mind, which is what the whole passage is doing. This is the too-narrow trap.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker is crossing a city bridge that the speaker's father inspected for many years.

Each morning the bridge takes the weight of the city:
trucks of lettuce, the school bus, a man with a cello.
It does not complain. It was built to flex,
to give an inch in August and take it back in frost.
My father checked its rivets for thirty years.
I used to think him rigid, a man of fixed numbers.
Only now, crossing it, do I see what he knew:
that holding firm means learning when to bend.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker realizes that the father, once thought rigid, understood the strength in bending.
The speaker lists the many vehicles and travelers that cross the city bridge each morning.
The speaker resents the years the father spent inspecting the bridge instead of being home.
The speaker admires the bridge's fixed design and wishes the father had been as unbending.
items.explanation: Put the poem into plain English first. A bridge carries the city's traffic and is built to flex with the seasons. The speaker's father inspected it, and the speaker once thought of him as rigid. The turn comes at 'Only now...do I see': crossing the bridge, the speaker understands that the father knew 'holding firm means learning when to bend.' A captures that change in how the speaker sees the father.

B.why: This only describes the images in the opening lines. It misses the reflection about the father that the poem turns to at the end. You read the setup and treated it as the point.

C.why: The poem never says the father was away from home, and it never shows the speaker feeling resentful. You added a grievance the text doesn't contain.

D.why: The bridge was 'built to flex,' so it isn't fixed. And the speaker comes to value bending, not being unbending. This choice turns both halves of the poem around.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of a fiction or poetry excerpt
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a novel. Anil, a graduate student in linguistics, is recording his grandmother, one of the last speakers of her village's dialect.

Anil had come with a list of four hundred words and a recorder charged overnight. His grandmother answered the first dozen patiently (water, smoke, the word for a younger brother) and then set the list aside. She wanted to tell him instead about the flood year, when the river took the mill. Anil glanced at the blinking red light, then at his unfinished columns. He let the list slide to the floor. Somewhere in her story, he realized, were words no list would have thought to ask for.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Anil drops his planned word list, sensing that his grandmother's story holds more of her language.
Anil grows impatient when his grandmother drifts away from the word list he has prepared.
Anil's grandmother refuses the word list because she distrusts the recorder he has brought.
Anil's grandmother describes a flood year in which the river carried away the village mill.
items.explanation: The introduction tells you the situation: Anil is recording a dialect that is disappearing. Follow what he does. He arrives with a long list, his grandmother sets it aside to tell a story, and he lets the list 'slide to the floor.' The last sentence names what he has realized: her story contains words his list would never have asked for. A matches both what he does and why he does it.

B.why: Anil does look at his unfinished columns, but he doesn't become impatient. He gives up the list and sees the value in her story. This choice reverses his reaction.

C.why: The grandmother does set the list aside, but the text gives her reason: she wants to tell a story. Nothing says she distrusts the recorder. You supplied a motive the passage never states.

D.why: This is accurate, but it is only the subject of the grandmother's story. It leaves out Anil's decision and what he realizes, which is what the passage as a whole is about. This is the too-narrow trap.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Mara Lindqvist's 2019 novel *The Grid*. Teodora, a city planner, is visiting a public square she designed ten years earlier.

Teodora had drawn every bench on this square herself, angling each one toward the fountain so that strangers would sit side by side and watch the water. Now she found the benches dragged into loose circles, turned toward one another, the fountain behind them ignored. A boy had chalked a hopscotch court across her careful paving. She had expected to feel slighted. Instead she stood a long while at the edge of the square and felt, absurdly, that she had been thanked.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Teodora resents that residents have ignored the layout she planned and rearranged the square without her approval.
Teodora finds that residents' changes to the square she designed leave her unexpectedly gratified rather than offended.
Teodora originally placed the benches facing the fountain so that strangers would sit together and watch the water.
Teodora decides that future squares she designs should leave residents free to arrange the benches however they like.
items.explanation: Follow Teodora's feeling from start to end. She sees her design undone and 'had expected to feel slighted', but the final sentence turns: 'Instead' she feels 'that she had been thanked'. Choice B gets both the situation (residents have changed her square) and the direction of the feeling (gratified, not offended). The last sentence adds up the scene, and B is the only choice that matches it.

A.why: You took the feeling Teodora expected to have and treated it as the one she actually has. The word 'Instead' tells you she did not feel slighted. She felt thanked.

C.why: This is true, but it only describes the first sentence. It says nothing about what Teodora finds now or how she feels about it, and that is what the passage is about. It's too narrow.

D.why: You gave Teodora a plan the text never mentions. She stands and reflects, but she never decides anything about future designs.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Jonas Okafor's 1958 short story "Piece Rate." Ruth works at a sewing machine in a shirt factory.

For eleven years Ruth had paid herself in shirts. Every collar she finished was worth a few cents, and by noon she could tell from the pile at her elbow whether the week's rent was safe. The new manager meant the hourly wage as a kindness, and the others welcomed it. But at her machine Ruth found that the pile meant nothing now. The clock paid her the same whether she hurried or not, and she could not decide whether that made her free or simply lost.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ruth joins her coworkers in welcoming the new hourly wage as a relief from years of anxious counting.
Ruth secretly keeps working at her old pace to protest the manager's decision to change the way she is paid.
Under the old system, Ruth's weekly pay depended on how many shirts she managed to finish at her machine.
Ruth is unsettled by the switch to hourly pay because her familiar way of measuring her work no longer applies.
items.explanation: The introduction places Ruth at a factory machine. The passage then follows her from confident counting ('she could tell... whether the week's rent was safe') to confusion after the change: 'the pile meant nothing now', and she feels perhaps 'simply lost'. Choice D matches both the situation (the change to hourly pay) and the direction of her feeling (unsettled).

A.why: The text says 'the others welcomed it.' Then 'But' separates Ruth from them. You applied the coworkers' feeling to Ruth and reversed her tone.

B.why: You added a motive the text never gives. Nothing suggests that Ruth is protesting or hiding anything. She simply can't tell what the new pay means for her.

C.why: This is accurate, but it only covers the background in the first two sentences. It leaves out the change and Ruth's reaction to it, which is where the passage is heading. It's too narrow.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Elena Varga's 2011 poem "Field Notes." The speaker is a linguist recording one of the last speakers of a language.

I came with a recorder and a list:
the word for river, for grandmother, for rain.
Old Ilona gave them gladly,
spelling each one twice into the hum.
I filed them by evening, neat as seeds.
Only when the tapes played in a quiet room
did I hear what the list had left out—
her laughing between the words,
the song she hummed while she thought—
and know I had kept the words and lost the talk.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker realizes that a careful record of individual words missed the living speech that surrounded them.
The speaker describes collecting and filing a list of everyday words given by an elderly speaker of a language.
The speaker celebrates having fully preserved Ilona's language so that future listeners can still hear it spoken.
The speaker resolves to return to Ilona and record her songs before they are forgotten by the next generation.
items.explanation: Put the poem into plain English first. The speaker collects words efficiently, and then, 'Only when' the tapes play back, notices the laughter and humming that the list left out. The last line, 'kept the words and lost the talk', is the turn the poem builds toward. Choice A states that realization and covers the whole poem.

B.why: This describes only the first five lines, the collecting and filing. It misses the reflection the poem turns to after 'Only when', which is the point of the poem.

C.why: This reverses the tone. The speaker says the language was not fully preserved: she 'lost the talk'. The ending is regret, not celebration.

D.why: You added a plan the poem never mentions. The speaker recognises what is missing but never says she will go back or do anything about it.

The following text is adapted from a 2021 novel. Ines, a graduate student, is spending her first summer working at an archaeological excavation in southern Spain.

Before she came, Ines had pictured discovery as a flash of gold in the dirt, the kind of find that ends up behind museum glass. By August she had found no gold at all. What she found instead, on an ordinary Tuesday, was a shard of a cooking pot with a small thumbprint pressed into its rim, left by someone who had lifted it while the clay was still soft. She held it longer than she had held anything all summer. The gold she had imagined, she realized, would never have felt this close.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ines is disappointed that her first summer has turned up nothing but ordinary cooking pottery.
Ines keeps the marked shard to herself so that she can study it without her supervisors.
Ines finds that a modest object moves her more deeply than the treasure she once imagined.
Ines notices that the cooking pot was handled by its maker while the clay was still soft.
items.explanation: Follow how Ines feels from start to finish. She begins by imagining gold, finds only a plain shard with a thumbprint, holds it 'longer than she had held anything all summer,' and ends by realizing the gold 'would never have felt this close.' The passage turns on the gap between what she expected and what she found, and that gap comes out in favor of the humble object. Choice C covers both halves of that comparison and the feeling the final sentence names.

A.why: You reversed the tone. Ines does find only a cooking pot and no gold, but the passage says the shard affects her more than gold would have. She is moved, not disappointed.

B.why: You added a motive the text never gives. Nothing in the passage says Ines hides the shard or wants to keep it from anyone. She simply holds it for a long time.

D.why: You chose a detail that is true but too narrow. The text does say the clay was soft when the thumbprint was made, but that is one sentence. It leaves out the comparison with the gold she imagined, which is the point of the passage.

The following text is from a 2017 poem. The speaker describes a quilt made by the speaker's grandmother.

As a child I counted its squares for sleep:
the blue of a work shirt, a curtain's faded rose,
a yellow torn from some forgotten apron.
It was a blanket, and blankets were for warmth.
Years later, sorting her letters, I found the shirt
in a photograph, the apron at a wedding,
and then, only then, I understood
she had been writing her life in cloth
and I had slept beneath the pages.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker comes to see that a quilt once valued only for warmth records the grandmother's life.
The speaker recalls the colors of the quilt's squares and how counting them brought sleep in childhood.
The speaker is troubled to learn from the letters that the grandmother kept her past from the family.
The speaker discovers that the quilt's fabrics had little to do with anything in the grandmother's past.
items.explanation: First put the whole poem into plain English. As a child, the speaker thought of the quilt as just a blanket 'for warmth.' Years later, the speaker finds the same fabrics in old photographs and, 'then, only then,' understands that the grandmother had been 'writing her life in cloth.' The poem compares two ways of seeing the same object, and the main idea is the change between them. Choice A captures both the earlier view and the later one.

B.why: You described only the opening images. Counting the squares at bedtime is what the poem starts with, but it misses the 'then, only then' turn, where the speaker realizes what the quilt meant.

C.why: You added a motive the poem never gives. The letters and photographs show where the fabrics came from. Nothing suggests the grandmother hid her past, and the speaker is not troubled.

D.why: You reversed what the speaker finds. The shirt and apron show up in photographs from the grandmother's life, so the fabrics are tied directly to her past. That connection is the whole point of the ending.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a 2015 memoir. The author, a linguist, describes returning to the island where the author grew up to record the speech of older residents.

At university I learned to describe my grandmother's speech in the tidy terms of the field: a dropped final consonant, a vowel that rose where the mainland's fell. I could chart such features in an afternoon. Yet when I sat in Mrs. Doyle's kitchen with the recorder running, the charts seemed thin. She paused before certain words the way you might pause at a grave, and no column in my notes had room for that. I went home with forty hours of tape, convinced I had captured the sounds and missed the speech.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The author is pleased that years of academic training made a complete record of the island's speech possible.
The author learns that island speakers raise certain vowels in places where mainland speakers lower them.
The author abandons the study of linguistics after deciding that its methods are of no real use on the island.
The author realizes that the methods of the field capture the sounds of the dialect but not its deeper meaning.
items.explanation: Follow the author from beginning to end. At first the training seems powerful ('I could chart such features in an afternoon'). In Mrs. Doyle's kitchen the charts 'seemed thin,' and the last sentence sums it up: the author 'captured the sounds and missed the speech.' The passage is about the gap between what the methods can record and what the speech means to the people who use it. Choice D states both sides of that gap.

A.why: You reversed the tone. The author leaves feeling that the record is incomplete, not pleased with it. The final sentence says the 'speech' was missed even though forty hours of sound were recorded.

B.why: You picked a detail that is true but too narrow. The vowel difference is one example from the first sentence. It is not the author's realization about what the methods miss.

C.why: You went further than the text does. The author finds the methods incomplete, not useless, and nothing says the author gives up linguistics. The author leaves with forty hours of tape.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from a novel. Marguerite Osei, a civil engineer, attends the opening ceremony for a railway viaduct she designed.

The mayor's speech ran long, the band played twice, and someone pressed a ribbon of ceremonial silk into Osei's hand. She held it without looking at it. When the first freight train eased onto the span, the crowd cheered; Osei did not. She had gone down to the riverbank, where she stood with one palm flat against the nearest stone pier. Through the stone she felt the load arrive, settle, and pass, exactly as she had known it would. Only then did she smile, and only then did she climb back up to the platform, where the applause had already ended.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Although Osei is honored at the opening, the satisfaction she wants comes from feeling the viaduct carry its load as she planned, not from the public celebration.
Although Osei is honored at the opening, she slips away from the crowd because she fears the viaduct may not hold the weight of the first train.
Osei finds the opening ceremony tedious and resents the mayor for delaying the moment when the first train is finally allowed to cross the viaduct.
Osei is so moved by the crowd's cheering for the viaduct that she has to step down to the riverbank to compose herself before returning to the platform.
items.explanation: Start with the italic introduction: Osei designed the viaduct, and this is its opening. Then follow what she does from start to end. She holds the ceremonial ribbon without looking at it. She does not cheer. She goes down to the pier to feel the train cross, which happens "exactly as she had known it would." She smiles only after that, and by the time she climbs back up, the applause has ended. So her satisfaction comes from feeling the structure perform as she planned, not from the ceremony. Choice A covers the honor, where her attention goes, and why she smiles.

B.why: You correctly saw that Osei separates herself from the celebration, then explained it with the motive that seemed most likely: nerves. The text rules that out. She felt the load pass "exactly as she had known it would," so she had no doubt to resolve. The first half of this choice is right and the second half adds a fear the passage never gives her. Read every choice to the end.

C.why: You noticed that the speech "ran long" and that Osei ignores the ribbon, and you read her detachment as boredom and resentment. The text never says she is annoyed with the mayor or anyone else. Her attention is on the bridge, not against the ceremony. This choice adds a motive the text never gives.

D.why: This reverses the tone. The text says that when the crowd cheered, "Osei did not," and she goes to the riverbank to feel the train cross, not to recover from the cheering. She misses the applause altogether, so it cannot be what moved her.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker is an archaeologist excavating the remains of an ancient settlement.

I logged the sherds by depth and grid and hue,
bagged bone and charcoal, numbered every stone,
and wrote the site as something I could know
the way one knows a ledger or a map.
Then, under the lip of a broken jar,
a thumbprint, pressed in clay three thousand years
before my glove: some potter's careless mark.
I set my pencil down. The grid stayed true,
but I could not go back to counting what
I'd measured; someone's hand had measured me.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a novel. In the 1950s, Ruth Okafor works as a nurse in a rural vaccination campaign.

By Friday the ledger showed 412 children inoculated, more than any other district on the coast, and Dr. Mensah had written "Excellent" across the bottom in red. items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ruth takes quiet pride in her district's record, which her supervisor has praised as the best result anywhere on the coast.
Ruth worries that Dr. Mensah's praise will be withdrawn once he learns that a mother on the ridge road refused the vaccine.
Although her campaign has been officially praised, Ruth's thoughts keep returning to the one child she was unable to vaccinate.
Ruth is troubled that her ledger leaves out the boy, and she resolves to change how the campaign records families who refuse.
items.explanation: Follow Ruth from start to finish. The praise comes first, and then 'Yet' turns to what she actually dwells on: 'not 412 but one,' the boy she couldn't reach. Her wish that the ledger had a column for him shows that this one child, not the record, is what stays with her. Only this choice covers both the praise and where her thoughts turn after it.

A.why: You stopped before 'Yet.' The praise and the record are real, but the passage turns away from them. Ruth is not proud. She is preoccupied with the child she missed, so this choice reverses her feeling.

B.why: You gave Ruth a motive the text never mentions. Nothing suggests she is hiding the refusal or fears losing the praise. Her concern is the boy, not her standing with Dr. Mensah.

The following text is from a poem. The speaker describes a night spent at a backyard telescope.

I logged them as my father taught me:
magnitude, the hour, the patient drift
of Vega past the maple's highest limb.
I kept the columns neat, the pencil sharp.
It was near dawn, the eyepiece cold with dew,
before I looked down at the page and saw
the slant of every figure was his slant,
the night's whole log was in his hand
as much as mine.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker describes the methodical way of recording the brightness and movement of stars that a father once taught.
The speaker comes to see that a night of careful stargazing has also been a way of carrying on a father's practice.
The speaker regrets spending a whole night filling columns with figures instead of simply looking up at the stars.
The speaker comes to see that a father's habits have kept the speaker from developing a way of observing of the speaker's own.
items.explanation: Restate the poem in plain English. I logged the stars the way my father taught me, and near dawn I saw that my handwriting was his, so the log was as much his as mine. The turn at 'before I looked down' is a recognition: the speaker's careful observing carries the father's practice forward. Nothing in the poem says this is a loss.

A.why: You summarized the opening lines and skipped the turn. The poem's point is what the speaker realizes near dawn, not the method of logging.

C.why: You added a regret the poem doesn't contain. The speaker keeps the columns 'neat' and 'sharp' with no sign of wishing the night had gone differently, and the ending is a discovery, not a complaint.

D.why: You caught the turn toward the father and then gave it the wrong meaning. Seeing his hand in the log is not presented as a limitation. Nothing says the speaker has been held back from an independent style.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a memoir. As a teenager, the narrator joined a volunteer bird survey on a coastal marsh.

I had come for herons, or at least an osprey, and by the third morning I had counted nothing but sparrows: brown, quick, maddeningly alike. Mr. Haskell, who ran the survey, handed me his own field guide without comment. I began to notice the streaked breast of one, the yellow fleck above the eye of another, the way a third flicked its tail twice before it flew. By the end of the week I had stopped looking up at the sky at all.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Disappointed at first by the lack of rare birds, the narrator gradually becomes absorbed in the differences among the common ones.
Disappointed at first by the lack of rare birds, the narrator grows too discouraged by the week's end to keep scanning the sky.
With the help of Mr. Haskell's field guide, the narrator learns to identify several species of sparrow found on a coastal marsh.
Resenting Mr. Haskell for assigning a newcomer to sparrows, the narrator spends the week counting birds without much interest.
items.explanation: Trace the emotion. It starts as frustration ('maddeningly alike') and moves into close, specific noticing: the streaked breast, the yellow fleck, the double tail flick. The final line confirms the change. The narrator stopped looking up for herons because the sparrows below had become absorbing.

B.why: You read the last sentence literally and stopped there. The narrator did stop looking at the sky, but out of absorption, not discouragement. The sentences right before it show growing attention, which reverses the tone this choice gives.

C.why: This is roughly true but too narrow. It names what the narrator learned and leaves out the change in feeling from disappointment to absorption, which is what the passage is about.

D.why: You invented a grievance. Mr. Haskell only hands over a field guide, and the narrator's interest grows. It doesn't stay low.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from a short story. Archaeologist Lena Varga has spent eleven seasons searching for a ruler's tomb.

The trench opened not onto a burial chamber but onto a kitchen: a hearth ringed with soot, three cracked storage jars, a grinding stone worn into a shallow bowl. Her students were careful with her that evening, speaking softly, as one does around a loss. Lena let them. She did not explain that she had spent the afternoon with her palm pressed to the hollow of that stone, fitting her hand to the shape another hand had made, and that she had not wanted a king for hours.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Although Lena hides her disappointment from her students, failing to find the tomb after eleven seasons weighs heavily on her.
Although Lena is moved by the find, she hides this from her students because she fears they will think her long search was wasted.
Although the trench held no tomb, it revealed a hearth, storage jars, and a grinding stone used by the valley's ordinary residents.
Although her students assume the find is a disappointment, Lena is deeply absorbed by the traces of ordinary life it reveals.
items.explanation: The students treat the evening 'as one does around a loss,' but the last sentence shows what Lena actually felt. She spent the afternoon fitting her hand to the worn stone and 'had not wanted a king for hours.' The passage turns on the gap between what the others assume and what she feels.

A.why: You took the students' view as Lena's. The final sentence shows she isn't grieving at all, so this reverses her feeling.

B.why: The first half is right. She is moved, and she doesn't tell her students. But the text never says why she stays silent. The fear that her search will look wasted is a motive you supplied.

C.why: This lists what the trench contained and leaves Lena out entirely. A literary main idea has to cover the character's response, and that response is the point of the passage.

The following text is adapted from a novel. Tomasz's textile mill has just stopped paying workers by the piece and begun paying them by the hour.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

Though Tomasz earns more under the new system, he senses that something has gone out of his work now that it is no longer counted.

Tomasz checks the foreman's arithmetic and confirms that the new hourly wage is higher than his average at the old piece rate.

The following text is from a poem. The speaker works in a laboratory that measures the nutrients in food.

All week I weigh the lentils into grams,

choices: The speaker describes the laboratory process of reducing lentils to ash in order to measure the minerals they contain.
The speaker regrets that a mother who never weighed food could not give her children the nutrients a laboratory would advise.
The speaker comes to regard a mother's untrained way of feeding the family as its own kind of careful measurement.
The speaker comes to regard a mother's untrained way of feeding the family as more accurate than the laboratory's methods.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

Hester resents the commission for flooding the valley and keeps her field copy as proof that the official map is inaccurate.
Hester gives the commission the contours and property lines it requires for a valley that will be under water by spring.
Hester records the valley's daily life beyond her official task and treasures that record even after it is cut from the map.
